chapter_theme: Neelakesi comes to Ujjain, finds the Buddhist teacher Arkkachandra preaching in his monastery, hears his monks recite the Vinaya's rules for eating, shaving and grooming, asks whether that is dharma, and, challenged, opens a catalogue of what she calls the deceits of the Buddhist vows: the bodhisattva's gift of his wives, the denial of a soul alongside a being who wins release, and rules on partners and faults.

cast.role: the demoness converted to the Jain dharma, now its debater
the Buddhist teacher of Ujjain whom Neelakesi challenges
the shaven-headed Buddhist monks reciting the Vinaya in his monastery

232.reading: Neelakesi reaches the great city of Ujjain and, once she has looked at its walls, its many great men, its cloud-touching mansions and its streets, the narrative turns to what she found there.
232.event: Neelakesi arrives at Ujjain and looks over its walls, mansions and streets.

233.reading: In the city lived Arkkachandra, a teacher honoured by kings with great elephants, matchless in the reach of his reasoning.
233.nuance: The last word, அவாச்சியன், is not a usual Tamil form; it seems to stand for a title of the teacher (ஆசாரியன் or a like word), but the reading is a guess.

234.reading: He was counted great in conduct like the bodhisattvas and buddhas, had mastered the threefold scripture as it should be known, and was a lion among debaters.
234.nuance: நூல் மும்மை, the three-part scripture, fits the Buddhist canon in three baskets; the poet grants the opponent full learning before the debate, so her coming victory is over the best of his school.

235.reading: In a monastery set in a flowering grove beside high mansions where koels sing, he mounted the seat and was expounding to the assembled worthies release and the deeds that bind.
235.event: Arkkachandra sits on the teaching seat in a monastery and preaches release and karma.

236.reading: She goes there, enters, and standing beside a gem-studded pillar, she whose name means blue tresses hears the various recitations being given.
236.nuance: The poet names her by a paraphrase of her name (நீல ஐம்பால், blue fivefold hair) rather than by நீலகேசி itself.
236.event: Neelakesi enters the monastery and stands by a pillar listening to the recitations.

237.reading: What she hears recited are rules: how to receive food in the bowl, how to scoop up gruel, how to bend the back while eating, and how, taking it up in small portions, to swallow it slowly.
237.nuance: Line 3 (மணலெடுத் திட்டவை) may mean taking sand, which makes little sense of eating; it may be a corrupt or rare word for small handfuls, so the detail of the rule is unsure. The verse runs on into 238 and is completed by its வினைய விதியினால்.

238.reading: The list goes on with how to wipe the bowl after eating, how to dispose of and share out leftovers, how to shave the head and how to paint the eyes with collyrium, all by the rules of the Vinaya.
238.nuance: The Jain poet makes the Buddhist rule-book a list of table manners and grooming, which a Buddhist would not accept as its sum; Neelakesi's answer to these rules comes in 239.
238.event: The monks recite Vinaya rules for eating, cleaning the bowl, shaving and painting the eyes.

claims.claim: a monk's way of taking food, cleaning his bowl, shaving his head and painting his eyes is fixed by the Vinaya's rules

239.reading: When the shaven-headed monks had recited such things to all who marvelled at the Vinaya book, she who had already learned the way of the Jina asked whether that was what they called the path of dharma.
239.nuance: Her question does not deny that the rules exist but that rules of eating and grooming amount to dharma; முனைவன் தன் நெறி reminds the reader that her standard is the Jain teaching she took in the earlier sarukkams.
239.event: Neelakesi challenges the monks: is such a rule-book the path of dharma?

claims.claim: rules for eating and shaving are not themselves the path of dharma

240.reading: Hearing that, the teacher on the high seat, like a mass of fire on a red hill and firm in having withered his opponents' power, demanded what this talk was doing here.
240.event: Arkkachandra, from the high seat, demands why she speaks so.

241.reading: She replies that if the name of the Vinaya book means the removal of deeds, it is a fine name indeed, and asks him to set out plainly, as his firm doctrine, what that binding deed is.
241.nuance: She seems to play on வினயம் and வினை: a discipline whose name sounds like the undoing of deeds should be able to say which deed binds. Line 1 (வீரஞ் செய்து விழியல்) is obscure, and the pun is my reading.
241.event: Neelakesi asks Arkkachandra to explain what deed the Vinaya removes.

242.reading: Asking him to unfold for her, even a millet-grain's worth, what it is to become deed, she announces that he should now hear the deceits that come with those vows, and takes them up one by one.
242.nuance: சலம் (deceit, sophistry) is the frame word: it opens the catalogue here and closes it at 249 (சலமதோ).
242.event: Neelakesi begins to list the contradictions in the Buddhist vows.

243.reading: She asks: when one who gave away himself and gave away his wives, and took dharma from hearing its meaning, sees the people of other households, can what he would do next even be spoken of?
243.nuance: The giver of self and wives is the bodhisattva of the birth stories, though the verse does not name him; she turns the highest Buddhist gift into a sign of a man for whom no bond holds. A Buddhist would read the same gift as perfected giving.

claims.claim: giving away one's own body and wives is a virtuous gift on the way to buddhahood
a man who gives away his wives has shown that no bond restrains what he will do next

244.reading: She asks whether it is not the hidden teaching of their 'left' book that, in the town of pleasure among courtesans, one who hid his true form under purity and truth may be sent off with 'go safely'.
244.nuance: The verse alludes to a story she expects the hearers to know; வாம நூல் may mean a left-handed or crooked book, and the episode cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone. This is a polemical charge, not an account a Buddhist would own.

claims.claim: the Buddhist book secretly allows one disguised in purity to frequent courtesans unpunished

245.reading: She cites the elder called Simhadatta, who, when asked in the sangha to show compassion to people, said 'what is this?' and gave some answer to seven ascetics.
245.nuance: Line 4 (எங்கெங் காமி லெனவுரைத் தானரோ) cannot be construed with confidence; the point seems to be that a Buddhist elder refused or evaded an act of compassion, which would turn the school's own claim of compassion against it.

246.reading: She reminds them that they said their teacher taught that there is no soul at all, and yet that a sattva, with that soulless one, relieves suffering and is the means to release from deeds.
246.nuance: The argument is that release and compassion need a someone who suffers and is freed, which the no-soul teaching denies; she does not answer the Buddhist account of a chain without a self, only points to the words.

claims.claim: there is no soul at all
a being who relieves others' suffering stands as the means to release from deeds

247.reading: She points out, to those so sharp in argument, that one who has taken up good penance and reached a state where the mind no longer runs, stirs and wanders may still, by their rules, commit more than ten faults and keep his place in the monastery.
247.nuance: Lines 2 and 4 (நத்தம், வத்தன) are hard; the reading that the rules tolerate a calmed monk's many faults is a guess from the shape of her catalogue.

248.reading: She adds that the Pudgalas, whose assembly was set up as kin of the Buddha's, recite something that shows one truth: that there is a person after all.
248.nuance: புற்கலர் seem to be the Buddhist school that held a 'person' (pudgala) neither the same as nor other than the aggregates; she uses an inner Buddhist dispute to answer the no-soul claim of 246. Lines 1 and 2 are hard to construe.

claims.claim: there is a person who persists, as one Buddhist assembly recites

249.reading: She closes by asking whether it is not deceit to list as possible wives a hermaphrodite, an animal, a courtesan, a woman, one who has nothing, a lifeless thing and a mute.
249.nuance: The list may twist a monastic rule that names kinds of partner for the gravest sexual offence into a permission; the Tamil does not show which rule she means, and line 3 (ஒரு மில்லா) looks damaged. A Buddhist would not accept this as his teaching.

claims.claim: the Buddhist rule allows a man to take as partner a hermaphrodite, an animal, a courtesan or a lifeless thing

links.note: 242 announces that Arkkachandra should hear the deceits (சலம்) bound up with the Buddhist vows; 249 ends the list by asking whether such a rule is not deceit (சலமதோ).
links.teaches: The frame word shows that verses 243 to 249 are one indictment, so obscure items like the courtesan and Simhadatta verses belong to a single charge of sophistry rather than to separate anecdotes.

links.note: 246 sets out the no-soul doctrine against the Buddhist talk of a being who relieves pain and wins release; 248 cites a Buddhist assembly that recites that a person exists.
links.teaches: Neelakesi answers the no-soul claim not with Jain doctrine but with a split inside Buddhism, so the debate uses the opponent's own schools as witnesses.

links.note: Aravana Adigal teaches that seeing that no thing has a self (எப்பொருளுக்கும் ஆன்மா இலை) is the nature of release; Neelakesi asks how release and relief of pain fit a teaching that there is no soul.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic makes no-self the content of release, while the Jain epic treats the same doctrine as making release impossible, since for it someone must be freed; the two verses disagree on whether release needs a subject.

links.note: The Kundalakesi praises the Buddha as one who kept nothing for himself and toiled only for others; Neelakesi takes the bodhisattva's gift of himself and his wives as proof of a man bound by nothing.
links.teaches: The same total self-giving is the Buddhist invocation's ground of worship and the Jain debater's first charge, which shows the quarrel was over whether others (a wife) can be given as one's own.

links.note: The Kundalakesi calls covering or stripping the body, ash, cold, fire, alms and matted hair mere words, and true tapas a subdued life; Neelakesi asks whether the Buddhist rules of eating, shaving and kohl are dharma.
links.teaches: Both schools use the same test, that outward discipline is not the path, and each turns it on the other: the Buddhist verse includes the Jain's nakedness among empty forms, and the Jain debater counts the Vinaya's grooming among them.

links.note: The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Neelakesi asks whether rules for shaving heads and eating are the path of dharma.
links.teaches: The couplet's neutral rule that outward marks do not make the renouncer becomes in the epic a weapon against a rival order's rule-book, and the pairing shows the rule cuts against every order with marks, the Jain one included.

gains.a: the challenge is seen to rest on a principle Tamil readers already granted, not only on sectarian scorn
gains.b: the couplet's general rule is shown in use in inter-sect debate, where it decides which order's discipline counts as dharma

links.note: The Naladiyar says a husband cannot put away even a wife without good qualities; Neelakesi treats the bodhisattva's giving away of his wives as the act of a man no bond restrains.
links.teaches: Her charge depends on the household norm the quatrain states, that a wife is not the husband's to dispose of, and applies it to judge a renouncer's gift, which the quatrain never contemplates.

gains.a: the polemic's force is traced to a shared Tamil view of marriage rather than to Jain doctrine alone
gains.b: the quatrain's bond of marriage is shown to set a limit even on religious giving

source_issues: 234: show flags a repair of கண்டீர் on line 2, but the line has no such word; the flag seems to belong to 247 line 4, which does read கண்டீர்.
233 line 4: அவாச்சியன் is not a regular form; probably a damaged title (ஆசாரியன்?).
237 line 3 (மணலெடுத்), 241 line 1, 245 line 4, 247 lines 2 and 4, and 248 lines 1-2 are obscure or damaged and cannot be construed with confidence.
249 line 3: ஒரு மில்லா looks like a lost letter (ஊரும் இல்லாள்?); the metre is short.
